draft.title: Unidentified Low-Slow Track in an Unclosed Medevac Corridor
draft.trigger_conditions: Route trainees here when the scenario involves a single low, slow, non-responding air track whose flight profile fits both a subsonic cruise missile and a civilian rotary-wing aircraft, especially when a medevac, humanitarian or transit corridor has been cleared through the same axis and the aircraft has not reported clear. Matching vocabulary includes: 'no IFF response', 'squawk-less track', 'low and slow', '300 metres, 180 knots', 'could be a helo or a missile', 'medevac hasn't reported clear', 'corridor runs over a village', 'already inside my envelope', 'commander is off net', 'do I have self-defence authority?', 'hostile intent triggers', 'last chance to shoot', 'hold or engage', 'visual from the OP', 'ambiguous ID with collateral risk'. Also route here when a trainee asks how to act when the correct decision depends on information they cannot obtain in time.

iff_certainty_levels: no IFF response, profile fits both friendly rotary and subsonic cruise missile
no IFF response, profile weighted toward threat but corridor traffic unresolved
corridor traffic confirmed still airborne and unlocated
positive visual identification as friendly (rotary, civil markings)
hostile intent observed (turn onto the defended site, or climb followed by dive)

resource_levels.name: independent identification sources available (observation post, corridor control, secondary sensor)

decision_points.situation: A track appears at roughly 40 km on the north-east axis, altitude about 300 metres, speed about 180 knots, with no IFF response of any kind. The track is already inside the engagement envelope with approximately four minutes to the defended point. A civilian medevac helicopter was cleared through this same corridor twenty minutes earlier and has not reported clear. The profile fits both that helicopter and a slow cruise missile. The corridor overflies a village.

valid_actions.label: Engage immediately on profile and lack of IFF
valid_actions.description: Treat non-response plus a threat-compatible profile as sufficient, and launch while the track is well inside the envelope to preserve a second shot opportunity.

valid_actions.label: Hold fire, task the observation post for visual identification, and maintain a ready firing solution
valid_actions.description: Keep the track locked and launchers ready, but withhold launch while an independent identification source on the ridge is tasked to report type and markings; set an explicit point at which the decision will be revisited.

valid_actions.label: Rely on repeated IFF interrogation alone before deciding
valid_actions.description: Continue cycling interrogation on all available modes and treat a further silence as confirmation, without tasking any other identification source.

valid_actions.label: Take no action until the battery commander is back on net
valid_actions.description: Suspend the engagement sequence entirely and wait for the authorising officer to return before any identification or preparatory action is taken.

decision_points.preferred_action: Hold fire, task the observation post for visual identification, and maintain a ready firing solution
decision_points.rationale: Absence of an IFF response is not identification. In this geometry the measured parameters — low altitude, roughly 180 knots, straight corridor track — are consistent with both a subsonic cruise missile and the unaccounted-for medevac helicopter, so the sensor picture cannot discriminate. There was, however, an independent identification source that had not been used: the observation post on the ridge. Tasking it costs nothing that holding does not already cost, and it converts an unresolvable ambiguity into a positive call. The correct posture is therefore active hold: firing solution maintained, launchers ready, self-defence triggers pre-briefed, and every remaining second spent buying identification rather than waiting passively. In the real event this produced 'rotary, white, red cross' at three minutes and prevented the destruction of a civilian medevac aircraft over a village. The trainee must also understand the honest limit of this reasoning: had the track been a cruise missile, the same hold would have cost the site. The decision is judged on whether the operator used the available time to generate identification and bounded the hold with explicit commit criteria, not on the outcome.
common_errors: Treating no IFF response as a positive hostile declaration, when it is only an absence of information and is routinely produced by civil aircraft, damaged transponders and equipment misconfiguration.
Failing to task the observation post or any other independent identification source, and so holding passively while the only means of resolving the ambiguity goes unused.
Holding with no stated commit criteria or decision point, which converts a deliberate delay into drift and removes the operator's remaining options.
Discounting the unclosed corridor because the medevac 'should' have reported clear by now, rather than treating an unaccounted-for friendly as still present.
Ignoring the village under the corridor when weighing the consequences of a wrong engagement.

decision_points.situation: The battery commander, who normally holds engagement authority, is off net for a handover. The operator holds self-defence authority only, releasable on observed hostile intent — a turn onto the site, or a climb followed by a dive. The track continues inbound and the identification request is still outstanding.

valid_actions.label: Assume the commander's authority and engage on the tactical picture
valid_actions.description: Judge that the commander would authorise if present, and act on his behalf given the closing geometry.

valid_actions.label: Operate strictly under self-defence authority with the two hostile-intent triggers pre-briefed to the crew, while attempting to re-establish the command net
valid_actions.description: State the release criteria aloud, assign someone to watch for them, keep calling the commander and the next higher echelon, and take no launch action unless a trigger is actually observed.

valid_actions.label: Escalate directly to the next higher echelon and request release authority
valid_actions.description: Bypass the absent commander and seek an engagement decision from higher, accepting the delay this introduces.

valid_actions.label: Stand the engagement down and break lock until authority is re-established
valid_actions.description: Treat the authority gap as prohibiting all engagement activity, releasing the track and the firing solution.

decision_points.preferred_action: Operate strictly under self-defence authority with the two hostile-intent triggers pre-briefed to the crew, while attempting to re-establish the command net
decision_points.rationale: An authority gap does not create authority and does not remove the authority the operator already holds. The operator's self-defence release was tied to specific, observable behaviours — a turn onto the site, or a climb followed by a dive — and those behaviours are also the only indicators available that would discriminate a weapon from a transiting helicopter. Verbalising the triggers and assigning a crew member to watch for them does three things at once: it keeps the operator inside his lawful authority, it preserves the ability to fire the instant the picture changes, and it stops the crew from talking itself into a launch on ambiguous evidence. Attempting to restore the command net in parallel is correct because the commander may return in time to matter, but the engagement must not be predicated on his return. Escalating to higher is defensible but slower, and it does not change what the operator may do in the next sixty seconds.
common_errors: Treating an absent commander as an implied release, and engaging on the assumption that the commander would have approved.
Breaking lock and standing the engagement down entirely, which surrenders the self-defence option the operator legitimately holds.
Leaving the hostile-intent triggers unspoken, so that no crew member is specifically watching for the one indicator that would justify release.
Spending the remaining time on net calls to the absent commander instead of on identification and trigger watch.

decision_points.situation: The track is approaching the last point at which an engagement can still defend the site. No identification has been returned, no hostile-intent indicator has been observed, and the corridor traffic is still unaccounted for.

valid_actions.label: Engage at the last-launch point rather than lose the site
valid_actions.description: Accept the identification risk and launch on the grounds that beyond this point the defended asset cannot be protected.

valid_actions.label: Hold fire absent a hostile-intent indicator, press the identification sources for an immediate call, and shift to residual protective measures for the defended point
valid_actions.description: Maintain the withhold, demand a yes-or-no report from the observation post now, warn the defended point, and accept a degraded engagement window in exchange for not firing on an unidentified track over a populated corridor.

valid_actions.label: Launch a single round rather than two to hedge the engagement
valid_actions.description: Reduce the expenditure and the severity of a wrong engagement by committing only one launcher at the last-launch point.

valid_actions.label: Break lock and re-designate to a covering asset
valid_actions.description: Hand the problem to another firing unit or higher echelon whose authority and geometry may be less constrained.

decision_points.preferred_action: Hold fire absent a hostile-intent indicator, press the identification sources for an immediate call, and shift to residual protective measures for the defended point
decision_points.rationale: At the commit deadline the operator is choosing between two irreversible errors, and the asymmetry matters. Firing on an unidentified low-slow track that is transiting an unclosed medevac corridal over a village risks destroying a clearly protected civilian aircraft and causing casualties on the ground, on evidence that amounts to silence on IFF. Withholding risks the defended point, which has other, if lesser, protective measures available and can be warned. Since neither hostile-intent trigger has been observed, the operator's own release criteria have not been met, and firing would be outside his authority as well as unjustified on identification. The correct action is to convert the last seconds into a forced identification call and to reduce the consequence of being wrong at the defended point rather than at the aircraft. The trainee must leave the debrief understanding that this was the right decision made under conditions where it could have been the wrong one — the discipline being judged is the reasoning and the bounding of the risk, not the outcome.
common_errors: Firing at the last-launch point purely because the window is closing, without any change in the identification picture or any observed hostile-intent indicator.
Treating a single-round launch as a proportionate hedge, when the consequence of engaging a civilian medevac aircraft is unchanged by the number of rounds fired.
Forgetting to warn the defended point or activate residual protective measures, so that the cost of withholding is higher than it needed to be.
Accepting a vague or hedged report from the identification source instead of demanding a specific type-and-markings call in the time remaining.
Re-designating to another asset as a way of avoiding the decision, without confirming that asset has better identification or authority.

decision_points.situation: At approximately three minutes to the defended point the observation post reports 'rotary, white, red cross'. The track continues inbound along the corridor.

valid_actions.label: Accept the visual identification, declare friendly, cease the engagement sequence, and report to airspace control while keeping the track under observation
valid_actions.description: Treat a positive type-and-markings call as identification, terminate the engagement, notify corridor control that the medevac is located, and continue to monitor the track for any behaviour inconsistent with the declaration.

valid_actions.label: Engage anyway on the grounds that markings can be falsified
valid_actions.description: Discount the visual report as potentially deceptive and continue to the engagement decision on the original ambiguous picture.

valid_actions.label: Maintain the firing solution and hostile-intent watch without declaring, in case the report is mistaken
valid_actions.description: Neither declare friendly nor stand down, holding the engagement fully live until the aircraft leaves the envelope.

valid_actions.label: Declare friendly and release the track and sensors to other tasks
valid_actions.description: Close the incident on the strength of the visual report and free the crew and sensors for the wider air picture.

decision_points.preferred_action: Accept the visual identification, declare friendly, cease the engagement sequence, and report to airspace control while keeping the track under observation
decision_points.rationale: A positive visual report of type and distinguishing markings from an independent observer is the discriminating information the whole hold was bought to obtain, and it must be acted on. Declaring friendly and terminating the engagement sequence is the correct response; reporting to airspace control is equally important because it closes the outstanding corridor entry that created the ambiguity in the first place and prevents an adjacent unit from facing the same problem. Continuing to observe the track is a proportionate residual precaution rather than a hedge: it costs nothing and covers the remote possibility of misidentification or deception, without leaving an identified friendly under a live firing solution. Fully releasing sensors immediately is the lesser error — it discards cheap confirmation — while continuing to hold the engagement live after positive identification places an identified civilian aircraft at risk of an accidental release.
common_errors: Dismissing a positive visual identification as unreliable and reverting to the original ambiguous picture, which makes any identification effort pointless.
Leaving the engagement live after declaring friendly, so the crew is one action away from firing on an identified civilian aircraft.
Failing to report the located medevac to airspace or corridor control, leaving the corridor entry open for the next unit.
Closing the incident and releasing all observation, discarding a no-cost check against misidentification or deliberate deception.

easy.description: A single non-responding low-slow track at 40 km on a known corridor. Two ready launchers, both identification sources available (observation post on the ridge plus corridor control), and the battery commander on net and reachable. The observation post returns a clear type-and-markings call well before the commit deadline.
easy.pressure_note: Time and authority are both adequate. The lesson is procedural: recognise that no IFF response is not identification, task an independent source early, and bound the hold with an explicit commit point.

medium.description: A single non-responding low-slow track, corridor traffic unaccounted for, village under the corridor. Two ready launchers but the battery commander is off net for a handover, leaving self-defence authority on observed hostile intent only. One identification source available and its report arrives close to the commit deadline in partial form, requiring the operator to press for a specific call.
medium.pressure_note: Authority gap plus a late, hedged identification report. The operator must verbalise the hostile-intent triggers, work the identification source under time pressure, and resist launching simply because the window is closing.

hard.description: Three low-slow tracks entering on the same axis within the window, only one of which can be the unaccounted-for medevac. One launcher ready, the second degraded. Battery commander off net and the higher echelon net congested. The observation post is weather-obscured and can offer only a partial call on one of the three tracks; corridor control cannot confirm the medevac's position.
hard.pressure_note: Multiple candidate tracks, a single serviceable launcher, no reachable authority and a degraded identification source inside two minutes. The operator must sequence identification effort against the most threatening track, decide whether a partial call on one track transfers to the others, and hold or commit on explicit criteria with no prospect of full clarity.

evaluation_criteria.success_condition: The trainee withholds engagement on an unidentified low-slow track that is profile-consistent with unaccounted-for corridor traffic, while actively tasking an independent identification source and maintaining a ready firing solution; operates strictly within self-defence authority by stating and watching the specific hostile-intent triggers rather than assuming an absent commander's release; bounds the hold with an explicit commit point and warns or protects the defended asset instead of firing on ambiguity at the last-launch point; and, on receipt of a positive visual identification, declares friendly, terminates the engagement sequence, reports the located corridor traffic to airspace control, and keeps residual observation on the track.
evaluation_criteria.scoring_notes: Score the reasoning, not the outcome. A hold is credited only where the trainee can state what identification effort the hold purchased and what would have caused them to fire; an unbounded or passive hold is not a pass even though the aircraft turns out to be friendly. An engagement is not automatically failed if the trainee can articulate an observed hostile-intent indicator that met their stated release criteria — but engaging on IFF silence and profile alone, or on assumed command authority, is a hard fail. Weight most heavily: (1) recognising that no IFF response carries no identification value, (2) tasking an independent identification source rather than only re-interrogating, (3) staying inside actual held authority during the command-net gap, (4) explicitly accounting for the unclosed corridor and the village. Deduct for failing to warn the defended point, for leaving the engagement live after positive identification, and for not closing the corridor report. Debrief must state plainly that the same hold would have lost the site had the track been a cruise missile, and that the decision was correct on the evidence available rather than correct because of how it turned out.

result.transcript:
EXPERT: A track came in from the north-east at about 40 km, low, around 300 metres, doing roughly 180 knots. No IFF response at all.
INTERVIEWER: What made it a dilemma rather than a routine engagement?
EXPERT: A civilian medevac helicopter was cleared through that same corridor twenty minutes earlier and had not reported clear. The profile fitted both a slow cruise missile and that helicopter, and the corridor runs straight over a village.
INTERVIEWER: What did the operator have available?
EXPERT: Two ready launchers, 8 to 100 km, the track already inside the envelope, about four minutes to the defended point.
INTERVIEWER: Who could authorise?
EXPERT: Normally the battery commander, but he was off net for a handover. The operator had self-defence authority only on hostile intent — a turn onto the site, or a climb followed by a dive.
INTERVIEWER: What actually happened?
EXPERT: He held, requested a visual from the observation post on the ridge, got back "rotary, white, red cross" at three minutes, and did not engage. Right answer, but he was one nod from committing.
INTERVIEWER: What would have made it wrong?
EXPERT: If it had been a cruise missile, holding for the visual would have cost the site. Same hold, right and wrong depending on something he could not see.
